Development · Planning · Draft

What should an operator development plan include?

A practical plan connects the role you need with the learning, practice, and evidence that support it.

The short answer

An operator development plan should define the target role, starting point, learning objectives, supervised practice, evaluation needs, evidence to retain, and next review. It should make responsibility for each step clear.

Seven parts of a useful plan

  1. The target role. Identify relevant equipment and the tasks you expect the employee to develop toward. Keep the scope specific.
  2. The starting point. Record relevant experience, completed learning, credentials, and known gaps. Distinguish reported experience from observed performance.
  3. Learning objectives. Set out the topics and knowledge checks that will prepare the employee for the next stage of practice.
  4. Supervised practice. Identify the trainer, practice objectives, equipment, and assignment limits. Follow the rules that apply to the work.
  5. Evaluation needs. Identify which demonstrations and evaluations are needed, who is responsible, and how gaps will be addressed.
  6. A connected record. Keep learning results, practice observations, evaluation evidence, and employer decisions accessible together.
  7. The next review. Name the owner of each follow-up action and set a review point. Update the plan when the equipment, work, or development needs change.

A simple way to review each step

Ask three questions: What is the objective? What evidence shows progress? What still needs attention? These questions keep the conversation useful for both the employee and the supervisor.

Separate development from authorization

Finishing a course or a practice objective does not authorize operation. Keep the employer’s qualification decision and work authorization distinct, with the assigned equipment and tasks clearly identified.

Start with one role

You do not need to map every job in the company before beginning. Choose one role, establish the starting point, and agree on the next learning and practice steps. Use what you learn from that process to refine the plan.

Sample / draft article. Prepared for this website preview; editorial and technical review are required before public publication. This is general development guidance, not a determination that a particular person is qualified or authorized.

Regulatory reference: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1427 — Operator training, certification, and evaluation. Source reviewed October 12, 2026.
